Good afternoon. Yesterday, in Class 10, you learned to rate the likelihood and the impact of a risk scenario: the scales, the qualitative and quantitative methods, the effects on confidentiality, integrity and availability, the complexity of exploitation and the spread of an attack through the network. Today you finish Topic 5. You will ask one more question before you accept an impact rating — how well could Kalmia respond if the scenario happened? Then you will put every rated scenario into one table, the risk register, and one picture, the risk matrix. Finally you will decide, with a written method, the order in which the risks receive attention.

Tonight is also a hand-over between two labs. Lab 2, the threat catalogue, is due tonight at 23:59. Lab 3, the risk register and its prioritization, starts now: the three outputs of tonight's examples are its first rows.

The one fact to remember

A risk is managed only when it is written in the register with its evidence, its owner and its rank.

Lesson 1 — The organization's ability to respond to an incident

Why response capability changes impact, what it is made of, how to measure it, and the legal clock in Québec
0:04 – 0:22

Lesson notes

▣ Slide 7 — Lesson 1 — The organization's ability to respond to an incident

Same attack, different outcome

▣ Slide 8 — Same attack, different outcome

Two coffee roasters of the same size are hit by the same ransomware on the same Saturday night. The first one has a written response plan, an alert that wakes someone up, and a backup copy kept away from the network; its order processing is back on Saturday evening. The second one has none of these; its staff discover the problem on Monday morning and the business is disrupted for almost a week. The threat, the vulnerability and the likelihood are identical. The impact is not.

This is the reason for tonight's first lesson. In Class 10 you rated the impact of each scenario under today's conditions. The size of the harm, however, depends on two measurable quantities: how long the disruption lasts and how far it spreads. Both depend on what the organization does after the event begins: how quickly it notices, how quickly it stops the spread, and how quickly it restores service. The ability to respond is therefore an input of the impact assessment, not a separate topic.

In the vocabulary of ISO 31000:2018, a control is any measure that maintains or modifies risk. Preventive controls mainly lower likelihood. The response capability of an organization is a set of detective and corrective controls: it mainly lowers impact, by reducing the duration and the extent of the damage. Competency EZ02 of your program asks for a realistic assessment of the ability to respond to an incident (criterion 4.6). Realistic means based on evidence, not on intentions: a backup that has never been restored is not yet a recovery capability.

Event, incident and incident response

▣ Slide 9 — Event, incident and incident response▣ Slide 10 — The response lifecycle and the CSF 2.0 Functions

Three words must be kept apart. A security event is any observable occurrence in a system or a network: a sign-in, a firewall block, a file change. Most events are harmless. A security incident is an occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or of a system, or that violates a security policy. Incident response is the organized set of actions taken to detect an incident, analyze it, contain it, eradicate its cause, recover normal operations, and learn from it.

NIST SP 800-61 Revision 3, published in April 2025, treats incident response as part of cybersecurity risk management and organizes its recommendations around the six Functions of the NIST CSF 2.0: Govern, Identify and Protect prepare the organization; Detect finds the adverse event; Respond analyzes, contains and eradicates; Recover restores; improvement (lessons learned) feeds back into Identify. The older lifecycle of Revision 2 (2012) — preparation; detection and analysis; containment, eradication and recovery; post-incident activity — is still the sequence used by most training material, including the videos below. The international standard ISO/IEC 27035-1:2023 describes the same logic as five phases: plan and prepare, detect and report, assess and decide, respond, learn lessons.

For a risk assessment the exact list of phases matters less than one fact: each phase takes time, and the sum of these times is the outage the business suffers.

What the ability to respond is made of: four components

▣ Slide 11 — Four components of the ability to respond

An organization's ability to respond can be described with four components. Each one can be observed and documented.

  • People — named roles (incident lead, technical responder, decision-maker, communication, privacy officer), a backup person for each role, and availability outside office hours. At Kalmia, KRF-32: one half-time IT (information technology) coordinator holds all network knowledge and passwords and has no backup.
  • Process — a written and approved incident response plan (IRP [incident response plan]); playbooks, which are step-by-step procedures for the most likely scenarios (ransomware, account takeover, payment fraud); escalation criteria; a contact list; who may decide to disconnect a system; message templates; evidence handling. At Kalmia, KRF-19: no incident response plan.
  • Technology — logs kept long enough and alerts that someone actually reads; the technical ability to isolate a device or a network zone; backups with a copy that an attacker on the network cannot reach, restored regularly as a test. At Kalmia, KRF-17: a flat network that cannot be partly isolated; KRF-21: a draft backup procedure, a backup disk that stays connected, and failures that nobody notices.
  • Partners and obligations — the incident clauses of the MSP (managed service provider) contract (hours, response time), cyber insurance, a forensic contact, the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security reporting form, the police for crimes, and the privacy regulator when personal information is involved. At Kalmia, InfoNord's contract covers the helpdesk during business hours only.

The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security guidance on incident response plans (ITSAP.40.003) lists the same elements for any organization — a response team with backup contacts, an approved policy, communication rules, response steps, reliable backups, training and exercises — and its baseline controls for small and medium organizations start with control BC.1, “develop an incident response plan”.

Measuring the ability to respond in hours

▣ Slide 12 — Measuring the ability to respond in hours▣ Slide 13 — The outage model: detect + contain + recover versus the MTD

Response capability is measured first in time. Five measures are used in reports and in this course:

  • MTTD (mean time to detect) — the average time between the start of an incident and its detection.
  • MTTC (mean time to contain) — the average time between detection and containment, the moment the damage stops spreading.
  • MTTR (mean time to recover) — the average time needed to restore normal service. The letters are also read “mean time to repair” or “to respond”: always define the term in your report.
  • RTO (recovery time objective) — the target maximum time to restore a system or a process after a disruption, set by the business impact analysis.
  • RPO (recovery point objective) — the maximum acceptable loss of data, measured in time (an RPO of 24 hours requires at least a daily backup).

Above them sits the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime): the longest time a business process can be unavailable before the harm becomes unacceptable. NIST SP 800-34 Revision 1 uses this term; ISO (International Organization for Standardization) 22301 calls it the MTPD (maximum tolerable period of disruption). The RTO (recovery time objective) must always be shorter than the MTD. For tonight's example, Karim Haddad sets the MTD of Kalmia's order processing at 48 hours: the wholesale clients receive their deliveries every week, and a longer stop means lost clients.

The model used in this course is a simple sum: outage ≈ time to detect + time to contain + time to recover. When the expected outage of a scenario is longer than the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of the process it stops, the operations dimension of the Kalmia impact scale is at least 4 (one to three days) and becomes 5 beyond three days.

MeasureQuestion it answersKalmia today (scenario R-01)
Time to detectWhen did we notice?53 h 20 min — found on Monday at 07:30
Time to containWhen did the damage stop spreading?8.5 h — nobody knew who may unplug NAS-01
Time to recoverWhen did the business work again?96 h — the connected backup disk was encrypted too
Outage (sum)How long did the business suffer?158 h, more than three times the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of 48 h

A realistic score: the readiness scorecard

▣ Slide 14 — A realistic score: the readiness scorecard (0 to 3)

To compare organizations, or the same organization before and after improvements, each capability receives a maturity score from 0 to 3. The scale below is a course rule inspired by maturity models; it is not a standard.

Eight capabilities are scored: (C1) the incident response plan and playbooks; (C2) roles, contacts and a backup person; (C3) detection, meaning alerts that are read; (C4) containment, meaning the ability to isolate; (C5) recovery, meaning an off-site or offline copy and tested restores; (C6) external support; (C7) legal and communication duties; (C8) exercises and lessons learned. The readiness score is the total divided by 24, expressed as a percentage: 0 to 33 % LOW, 34 to 66 % MODERATE, 67 to 100 % HIGH.

The evidence rule protects the score from optimism: a 3 requires the record of a test in the last 12 months — a restore log, an exercise report. The cheapest test is a tabletop exercise (TTX [tabletop exercise]): the team sits around a table, the facilitator describes a scenario minute by minute, and each person says what they would do. The gaps appear without any system being touched.

ScoreNameMeaning
0AbsentThe capability does not exist.
1InformalIt exists in someone's head, as a draft or as a habit; it is not written and approved, or it has a known weakness.
2DocumentedIt is written, approved by management and known by the people who must use it.
3TestedIt is documented and approved, and a test in the last 12 months (exercise, restore test) proved that it works.

The legal clock: Québec and Canada

▣ Slide 15 — The legal clock: Law 25 (Québec) and PIPEDA (Canada)

When personal information is involved, the law adds steps and deadlines to the response. In Québec, the Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector, as amended by Law 25, defines a confidentiality incident as the access, use or communication of personal information not authorized by law, or its loss. Since September 22, 2022, an enterprise that has reason to believe that such an incident occurred must take reasonable measures to reduce the risk of injury; if the incident presents a risk of serious injury, it must promptly notify the Commission d’accès à l’information (CAI) and the persons concerned; and it must keep a register of confidentiality incidents — all of them, including the minor ones — and send a copy to the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, the Québec privacy regulator) on request. The risk of serious injury is assessed from the sensitivity of the information, the anticipated consequences of its use, and the likelihood that it will be used for injurious purposes.

Federally, PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) requires an organization to report to the OPC (Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada) every breach of security safeguards that creates a real risk of significant harm (RROSH [real risk of significant harm]), to notify the affected individuals, and to keep a record of every breach for two years (OPC guidance). In a province such as Québec, which has its own private-sector law, PIPEDA mainly applies to federally regulated businesses and to personal information that crosses provincial or national borders in commercial activities. This is general information, not legal advice (Legal Notice, section 8.1).

For readiness the consequence is direct: the assessment of serious injury, the notices and the register must be done during the response, by named people. At Kalmia, unknown U-05 says that the serious-injury assessment of INC-04 was never documented. That is why capability C7 scores 1.

Key terms to learn

▣ Slide 16 — Key terms — Lesson 1
Security event
Any observable occurrence in a system or a network; most events are harmless.
Security incident
An occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or a system, or violates a security policy.
Incident response
The organized actions taken to detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover from and learn from an incident.
Response capability
The people, processes, technology and partners that let an organization respond; a set of detective and corrective controls that mainly reduces impact.
Incident response plan (IRP [incident response plan])
The written and approved document that sets roles, contacts, decisions, steps and communications for incidents.
Playbook
A step-by-step procedure for one type of incident, for example ransomware.
MTTD (mean time to detect) / MTTC (mean time to contain) / MTTR (mean time to recover)
Average times to detect, to contain and to recover; their sum approximates the outage.
RTO (recovery time objective) / RPO (recovery point objective)
Target time to restore a process; maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
MTD (maximum tolerable downtime)
The longest time a business process can be unavailable before the harm becomes unacceptable; the RTO (recovery time objective) must be shorter.
Readiness score
Course rule: sum of eight maturity scores (0–3) divided by 24; LOW, MODERATE or HIGH.
Tabletop exercise (TTX [tabletop exercise])
A discussion-based exercise in which the team walks through a scenario to test the plan.
Confidentiality incident
Under Québec law: unauthorized access to, use or communication of personal information, or its loss.
Register of confidentiality incidents
The legal register every Québec enterprise keeps of all its confidentiality incidents.

Micro-activity — Clock the outage (3 min)

▣ Slide 17 — Micro-activity — Clock the outage (3 min)

Incident INC-03 (August): a café's card payments stopped for two hours. The manager noticed after 20 minutes, called the POS (point of sale) provider, waited 40 minutes for an answer, and the service returned one hour later. (1) Split the two hours into detect, contain and recover. (2) Which capability of the scorecard would have shortened the first part? (3) Does the outage exceed what the café could tolerate if its MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) is four hours?

Show the answer

(1) Detect 20 min; contain (waiting for the provider to act) 40 min; recover 60 min — total 2 h. (2) C3, detection: a POS (point of sale) status alert to the manager's phone. (3) No: 2 h is below an MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of 4 h, so the operations dimension stays at 2 (a few hours, one site).

Real-life example 1 — Saturday, 02:10: ransomware on NAS-01. How long until Kalmia ships coffee again?

▣ Slide 19 — Real-life example 1 — Saturday 02:10, ransomware on NAS-01▣ Slide 20 — Real-life example 1 — the readiness scorecard, today and improved
Task of the example

Score Kalmia's ability to respond with the eight-capability scorecard, estimate the outage of scenario R-01 (ransomware encrypts the NAS-01 shares) today and after four improvements, compare each outage with the 48-hour MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of order processing, and derive the response-adjusted impact that goes into the Lab 3 register.

How it relates to this lecture

This is Lesson 1 applied: the four components (people, process, technology, partners), the maturity scale 0–3, the sum detect + contain + recover, the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime), and the impact dimensions of Class 10.

Where it goes next (future labs)

Lab 3: the columns “Response readiness” and “Impact justification” of every register row (ir_readiness.csv, ir_timeline.csv); the scorecard sheet of the Lab 3 workbook. Lab 4 — Risk treatment and prevention plan: the four improvements are candidate treatment actions; backups and continuity are covered in Class 13 (BCP [business continuity plan] and DRP [disaster recovery plan]). Integrative Project report: the section “Ability to respond”.

Lucas Martin works half-time, Monday to Friday. InfoNord's helpdesk answers during business hours. The backup disk of NAS-01 stays connected all the time. On Saturday at 02:10 a phished office PC (personal computer), compromised during the week, starts encrypting the shares of NAS-01. Nadia Roy asks a precise question: “If this happens, how long are we down, and what would change that number?”

CapabilityComponentTodayEvidence for today's scoreAfter the improvement
C1 Incident response plan and playbooksProcess0 — absentKRF-19: no plan exists2 — Write and approve a short plan with a ransomware playbook
C2 Roles, contacts and a backup personPeople1 — informalKRF-32: one half-time coordinator, no backup2 — Contact list with a backup for each role and an on-call number
C3 Detection: alerts read by someoneTechnology1 — informalMonitoring reports exist; nobody reads alerts outside office hours2 — Alert on mass file changes on NAS-01, sent to the on-call phone
C4 Containment: isolate a device or a zoneTechnology0 — absentKRF-17: flat network, no isolation procedure2 — Written isolation procedure; NAS-01 can be cut off remotely
C5 Recovery: off-site copy and tested restoreTechnology1 — informalKRF-21: draft procedure, backup disk always connected3 — Off-site copy every night; restore test every month
C6 External support: MSP (managed service provider), insurance, forensicsPartners1 — informalInfoNord helpdesk in business hours only2 — 24/7 incident clause added to the InfoNord contract
C7 Legal and communication (Law 25)Partners1 — informalU-05: INC-04 assessment not documented1 — (not part of tonight's four improvements)
C8 Exercises and lessons learnedProcess0 — absentNo exercise has ever been run1 — One tabletop exercise scheduled
Readiness score—5/24 = 20.8 % → LOW15/24 = 62.5 % → MODERATE

Today the outage of R-01 is about 158 hours (6.6 days): 53.3 h to detect, 8.5 h to contain, 96 h to recover. That is more than three times the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of 48 hours, so the operations dimension is 5 and the impact of R-01 stays at 5 (SLE [single loss expectancy] $150,000 = $250,000 × 0.60). With the four improvements — a written plan with an on-call number, an alert on mass file changes, an isolation procedure, and a tested off-site copy — the outage falls to about 16.8 hours (1.25 + 1.5 + 14), below the MTD; the operations dimension falls to 3, and the money dimension to 3 (SLE $25,000 = $250,000 × 0.10). The response-adjusted impact becomes 3 and the score of R-01 moves from 4 × 5 = 20 (CRITICAL) to 4 × 3 = 12 (HIGH). The likelihood does not change: the improvements do not stop the phishing e-mail. This is exactly what response capability does in a risk assessment.

Code example 1 — Readiness scorecard and outage clock (Python)

▣ Slide 21 — Code example 1 — readiness scorecard and outage clock (Python)
Task of the code

The script scores the eight response capabilities of Kalmia today and after the four improvements, computes the readiness percentage and level, adds up the three phases of the R-01 outage, compares the total with the 48-hour MTD (maximum tolerable downtime), converts outage, money and personal information into impact levels, keeps the highest one, and writes ir_readiness.csv and ir_timeline.csv for the Lab 3 register.

How it relates to the lecture

It is Lesson 1 in executable form: maturity scale, readiness levels, the sum detect + contain + recover, the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) test and the “highest dimension” rule of the Kalmia impact scale (Class 10).

Code example 1 — Readiness scorecard and outage clock (Python)
Execution window — every executed line and its output (pause to read)

    The replay shows a real execution of the script recorded on November 11, 2026 with Python 3.13 (standard library only). Run it yourself: python3 kalmia_ir_readiness.py. Outputs:

    Step by step — what the code does

    1. The script imports the csv module of the Python standard library; no extra package is needed (Python 3.8 or later).
    2. It defines the constants of the case: the 48-hour MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of order processing, the maturity names, the asset value of the NAS-01 data ($250,000) and the exposure factors agreed in Class 10 (0.60 today, 0.10 with a tested off-site copy).
    3. It lists the eight capabilities, each with its score today, its score after the improvements and the evidence for today's score — the KRF (Kalmia risk factor) rows of Class 9.
    4. It stores the three phases of the R-01 outage (detect, contain, recover) for both cases.
    5. Three small functions convert numbers into scale levels: readiness_level() turns a percentage into LOW, MODERATE or HIGH; operations_level() turns hours into the operations level of the impact scale; money_level() turns dollars into the money level.
    6. The main loop runs twice, once for “today” and once for “improved”. For each capability it reads the score, adds it to the total and prints one line; the visualization fills the bar of that capability.
    7. It computes the readiness percentage (total / 24) and its level, then the outage (sum of the three phases) and compares it with the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime); the timeline bars are drawn with the 48-hour line.
    8. It converts the outage, the single loss expectancy and the personal information (46 employees, level 2) into levels and keeps the highest one — the response-adjusted impact.
    9. It writes ir_readiness.csv (one row per capability) and ir_timeline.csv (one row per case) and prints the conclusion for R-01: impact 5 today, 3 after the improvements; score 20 → 12.
    10. Start runs the recorded execution line by line; Pause stops on the current line so that the variables can be discussed; Step advances one line; Restart clears the window and the drawing.

    Lesson 2 — The risk matrix and the risk register

    Reading and designing a 5 × 5 matrix, its limits, risk appetite, and the columns and rules of a correct register
    0:22 – 0:42

    Lesson notes

    ▣ Slide 23 — Lesson 2 — The risk matrix and the risk register

    From two ratings to one level: the Kalmia matrix

    ▣ Slide 24 — The Kalmia 5 × 5 matrix and its four bands▣ Slide 25 — Designing a matrix: grids, asymmetry, lookup tables

    A risk matrix, also called a heat map, is a grid that crosses the likelihood scale and the impact scale. Each of its cells receives a risk level. In Class 10 you built Kalmia's version: five likelihood levels, five impact levels, and a cell value equal to likelihood × impact, from 1 to 25. The value is read with four bands: 1 to 4 LOW, 5 to 9 MEDIUM, 10 to 16 HIGH, 20 to 25 CRITICAL. The products 17, 18 and 19 cannot occur on a 5 × 5 grid, so the last band starts at 20.

    To read the matrix, find the row of the likelihood level and the column of the impact level: the cell gives the score and the colour of the band. Tonight the matrix receives a second use. When the identifier of every rated scenario is written in its cell, the grid shows at one glance how the risks are distributed: how many sit in the CRITICAL corner, how many are HIGH because of a severe impact, how many because of a high frequency.

    Organizations design their matrices differently. Some use 3 × 3 or 4 × 4 grids. Some make the grid asymmetric, giving impact more weight than likelihood, so that every severe impact is at least HIGH. NIST SP 800-30 Revision 1 does not multiply numbers at all: its level-of-risk table combines the qualitative levels directly (Appendix I). The OWASP Risk Rating Methodology rates likelihood and impact from 0 to 9, groups them into LOW, MEDIUM and HIGH, and reads an overall severity in a 3 × 3 table. None of these designs is “the correct one”: what matters is that the scales and the bands are written down before the rating starts, and used the same way for every risk.

    What a matrix cannot do

    ▣ Slide 26 — What a matrix cannot do (Cox, 2008)

    A matrix is a communication tool with known mathematical limits. The likelihood and impact levels are ordinal numbers: they give an order, not a distance. Multiplying them is a convention; a score of 16 is not “twice” a score of 8.

    The peer-reviewed article What’s Wrong with Risk Matrices? (Cox, 2008) demonstrated two further problems. The first is range compression: very different risks can receive the same cell or the same band — at Kalmia, a 10 and a 16 are both HIGH. The second is that a matrix can, in some configurations, give a higher rating to a quantitatively smaller risk. The author concludes that matrices must be used with caution and with an explanation of the judgments built into them.

    Kalmia's register therefore keeps more than the colour. Every row keeps the likelihood and the impact separately, the score, the written justification of each rating with its evidence, and its confidence level. For the highest risks it adds the money estimate of Class 10 (ALE [annualized loss expectancy]). The matrix shows the picture; the register holds the reasons.

    Inherent, current, residual and target risk

    ▣ Slide 27 — Inherent, current, residual and target risk

    The same scenario can be rated at different moments, and a register must say which moment it describes.

    • Inherent risk — the level of risk if no control existed. It is mostly a theoretical reference that shows what the existing controls are worth.
    • Current risk — the level of risk with the controls that exist today. This is what a small organization such as Kalmia rates in its first register, and what Lab 3 asks for.
    • Residual risk — the risk that remains after risk treatment. It is estimated in Topic 6, when controls are chosen, and accepted formally by management.
    • Target risk — the level that management wants to reach, by a given date.

    Lesson 1 gave an example: R-01 is 20 today (current risk) and would be about 12 with the four response improvements — that 12 is a candidate residual risk, to be confirmed when the improvements exist.

    Risk appetite and risk tolerance

    ▣ Slide 28 — Risk appetite, risk tolerance and Kalmia's decision rules

    The bands of a matrix are not a law of nature; they express a management decision. The ISO (International Organization for Standardization) risk-management vocabulary (ISO 31073:2022) defines risk appetite as the amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain, and risk tolerance as the readiness of the organization or a stakeholder to bear a risk after treatment in order to reach its objectives. Appetite is a general statement; tolerance is narrower and often expressed as a limit for one objective or one category of risk.

    Kalmia's appetite statement, approved by Nadia Roy for this course, connects every band to an action and a deadline: LOW risks are accepted and monitored, with a yearly review; MEDIUM risks receive an owner and a treatment decision within 90 days; HIGH risks require a treatment plan within 30 days and a monthly follow-up; CRITICAL risks require action within 7 days and a weekly report to the CEO (chief executive officer) until they fall to HIGH or lower. One tolerance statement completes it: no outage of order processing longer than 48 hours is tolerated — the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) of Lesson 1.

    A company with a low appetite places its band limits lower, so that more risks appear as HIGH or CRITICAL and receive attention; a company with a high appetite places them higher.

    BandScoresKalmia's decision ruleReview
    LOW1–4Accept and monitorEvery 12 months
    MEDIUM5–9Owner named; treatment decision within 90 daysEvery 6 months
    HIGH10–16Treatment plan within 30 days; monthly follow-upMonthly
    CRITICAL20–25Action within 7 days; weekly report to the CEO (chief executive officer)Weekly

    The risk register: definition and purpose

    ▣ Slide 29 — The risk register: definition and five purposes

    The ISO (International Organization for Standardization) vocabulary defines a risk register as a record of information about identified risks. In cybersecurity it is the one table in which every risk scenario is described, rated, owned, followed and finally closed. NIST IR 8286 Revision 1 and NIST IR 8286A Revision 1, both revised in December 2025, describe the cybersecurity risk register (CSRR [cybersecurity risk register]): each system or department keeps its register, and the most important rows roll up into the enterprise risk register that executives read. NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States) also publishes a schema for the register so that tools can exchange it.

    A register serves five purposes: decision (what to treat first), accountability (each risk has an owner), traceability (each rating points to its evidence), follow-up (status and review date) and communication (one table for management). It is a living document: Kalmia reviews HIGH and CRITICAL rows monthly and the others every six months, and after every incident or major change.

    The risk owner is the manager accountable for the risk and authorized to decide about it — not the technician who will apply a fix. At Kalmia the owners are Nadia Roy, Karim Haddad and Sophie Tremblay. Lucas Martin and InfoNord are the people who act; they are not the owners.

    The columns of Kalmia's register and a correct risk statement

    ▣ Slide 30 — The nineteen columns of the Lab 3 register▣ Slide 31 — Writing a risk scenario statement

    Kalmia's register — the format of Lab 3 — has nineteen columns in three groups. Identification: risk identifier, risk scenario, assets, threat, risk factors. Assessment: existing controls, likelihood and its justification, impact and its justification, response readiness, score, level, confidence, evidence. Decision and follow-up: owner, priority class and rank, status, review date. Score and level are always computed by a formula, never typed, so that they cannot contradict the ratings.

    The most important cell is the risk scenario statement. A useful statement names five elements in one sentence: the threat source, the threat event, the risk factor that makes it possible, the asset, and the consequence for the business. A simple template: “[Threat source] [does what] by exploiting [risk factor] on [asset], causing [consequence].”

    Compare. “Ransomware” is not a scenario: no asset, no weakness, no consequence. “Weak passwords” is a risk factor, not a risk. “A ransomware group enters through a phished office PC (personal computer), uses the shared NAS-01 administrator password and the flat HQ-LAN to reach NAS-01, and encrypts the shares and the connected backup disk, stopping order processing and production planning for several days and possibly copying HR (human resources) files.” is a scenario: it can be rated, owned and treated.

    Five quality rules apply to every row: one scenario per row; every rating has its evidence; the owner is a manager; the level agrees with the matrix; and the data stay fictional and confidential — the register of a real company is one of its most sensitive documents (Legal Notice, sections 6.7 and 17).

    Key terms to learn

    ▣ Slide 32 — Key terms — Lesson 2
    Risk matrix (heat map)
    A grid crossing likelihood and impact levels; each cell receives a risk level.
    Band
    A range of scores that receives one level and one decision rule (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL).
    Ordinal scale
    A scale whose numbers give an order but not a distance; multiplying ordinal levels is a convention.
    Range compression
    Different risks receiving the same cell or band, which hides real differences between them.
    Inherent / current / residual / target risk
    Risk without controls / with today's controls / after treatment / desired level by a date.
    Risk appetite
    The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain.
    Risk tolerance
    The readiness to bear a risk after treatment; a narrower limit for one objective or category.
    Risk register
    A record of information about identified risks; the one table where risks are described, rated, owned and followed.
    Cybersecurity risk register (CSRR [cybersecurity risk register])
    NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States)'s name for the register of cybersecurity risks that rolls up into the enterprise register.
    Risk owner
    The manager accountable for a risk and authorized to decide about it.
    Risk scenario statement
    One sentence naming threat source, event, risk factor, asset and consequence.
    Review date
    The date on which a row must be re-assessed; part of the follow-up columns.

    Code example 2 — Register builder, quality checker and heat map (Python)

    ▣ Slide 37 — Code example 2 — register builder, checker and heat map (Python)
    Task of the code

    The script reads the twelve seed scenarios from kalmia_seed_scenarios.csv, checks each row against Kalmia's quality rules (identifier, statement, assets, threat, ratings 1–5, justifications, evidence, owner, readiness, status, review date), computes the score and the level, places the identifier in its cell of the 5 × 5 matrix, writes kalmia_risk_register.csv and risk_matrix.csv, and prints the matrix and the result. With --lab3 it also enforces the Lab 3 minimum of twenty rows.

    How it relates to the lecture

    It applies Lesson 2 rule by rule: computed score and level, matrix bands, the owner rule, the evidence rule, and the heat map as a picture of the register.

    Code example 2 — Register builder, quality checker and heat map (Python)
    Execution window — every executed line and its output (pause to read)

      The replay shows a real execution of the script recorded on November 11, 2026 with Python 3.13 (standard library only). Run it yourself: python3 kalmia_risk_register.py (put kalmia_seed_scenarios.csv in the same folder). Outputs:

      Step by step — what the code does

      1. The script imports csv (to read and write the register), re (to check identifiers and dates) and sys (to read the command-line arguments).
      2. It defines the managers who can own a risk, the allowed readiness and status values, and the input file name (the seed file, or the file given on the command line).
      3. level_of() converts a score into the Kalmia band: 20 and above CRITICAL, 10 and above HIGH, 5 and above MEDIUM, otherwise LOW.
      4. check_row() applies the quality rules to one row and returns the list of problems; an empty list means the row is correct.
      5. The grid is a dictionary with one empty list for each of the 25 cells of the matrix. The file is then read: the header is the first line that names risk_id (a workbook export starts with title lines), the separator is the comma — or the semicolon used by French-language Excel — and rows without an identifier (the empty template rows of the workbook) are ignored.
      6. The main loop reads the rows one by one. For each row it converts likelihood and impact to integers, computes the score and the level, checks the row, and — when the row is correct — writes the identifier into its cell; the visualization places the chip on the heat map and adds the row to the register table.
      7. Rows with problems are printed with their problems and are not placed on the matrix, so that an incorrect rating never reaches the picture.
      8. After the loop the script writes kalmia_risk_register.csv (all columns plus score and level) and risk_matrix.csv (the 25 cells).
      9. It prints the matrix with likelihood 5 at the top, the counts per level and the result line: READY when every row passes (and, with --lab3, when there are at least twenty rows).
      10. Start, Pause, Step and Restart replay the recorded execution line by line; the variables of the current line are shown under the drawing.

      Lesson 3 — Prioritizing threats to assets

      Priority versus level, a documented ranking method with tie-breakers, priority classes, and threat signals (CVSS [Common Vulnerability Scoring System], EPSS [Exploit Prediction Scoring System], KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog], SSVC [Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization])
      0:42 – 0:56

      Lesson notes

      ▣ Slide 39 — Lesson 3 — Prioritizing threats to assets

      Why prioritize, and what a priority is

      ▣ Slide 40 — Why prioritize — and why a priority is not a level

      Kalmia has one half-time IT (information technology) coordinator, one managed service provider paid by the hour, and a limited budget. It cannot treat twelve risks at once. Prioritization is the documented ordering of risks for treatment, so that the risks with the greatest potential harm to the most important assets are treated first. Your program states it twice: criterion 4.1 of competency EZ02 asks for a “proper prioritization of threats to assets”, and the general criteria ask for “effective priority management”.

      A priority is not the same thing as a risk level. The level comes from the matrix. The priority adds what the matrix does not show: how critical the asset is, whether the threat is active right now, how ready the organization is to respond, and whether a deadline exists. NIST IR 8286B expresses the same idea: the priority of each cybersecurity risk is set in light of its potential impact on the objectives of the enterprise, and it is recorded in the register next to the risk.

      A good method has three properties: it is written before it is used, it gives the same order whoever applies it, and every position can be explained in one sentence to the owner.

      Kalmia's method: sort first, then break ties

      ▣ Slide 41 — Kalmia's method: sort first, then break ties

      Kalmia uses a lexicographic ordering: risks are sorted on a first criterion, and the next criterion is used only to separate risks that are equal on all the previous ones. This is the course rule for Lab 3.

      1. Priority class — P1 to P4, from the level and the escalation rule below.
      2. Score — higher first.
      3. Impact — higher first: between two equal scores, the worse consequence goes first.
      4. Asset criticality — from the business impact analysis of Lab 1: 3 (an outage stops production, sales or a legal obligation), 2 (a process is degraded but a workaround exists), 1 (limited effect).
      5. Threat evidence — a risk with active evidence goes first: a listing in the KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) catalogue, observed attack attempts, a Kalmia incident on the same asset in the last twelve months, or a weakness proven by a test.
      6. Response readiness — LOW before MODERATE before HIGH: the less ready the organization is, the sooner it must act.
      7. Identifier — only to make the order reproducible when everything else is equal.

      Asset criticality and threat evidence are recorded in two extra columns of the Lab 3 register — criticality and threat_evidence — next to the nineteen columns of Lesson 2.

      Applied to the three ties of Lesson 2: R-05 (2 × 5) goes before R-04 (5 × 2) because its impact is higher; R-08 goes before R-07 (both 12, impact 4, criticality 3) because the disk errors of MR-03 and the unclean shutdown of October 21 are active evidence, while ROAST-PC has none; R-06 goes before R-02 (both 16, impact 4) because the web shop is a critical asset and the loyalty database an important one.

      Priority classes, deadlines and the escalation rule

      ▣ Slide 42 — Priority classes, deadlines and the escalation rule

      Each band of the risk appetite (Lesson 2) becomes a priority class with a deadline counted from the date of the assessment, November 14, 2026: P1 — act within 7 days, weekly report to the CEO (chief executive officer); P2 — treatment plan within 30 days; P3 — treatment decision within 90 days; P4 — accept and monitor, review in 12 months. By default CRITICAL is P1, HIGH is P2, MEDIUM is P3 and LOW is P4.

      One escalation rule moves a HIGH risk to P1 when three conditions are all true: its score is 15 or more (the top of the HIGH band), there is active threat evidence, and the response readiness for this scenario is LOW. The rule exists because a risk that is both active and badly prepared will not wait 30 days. At Kalmia it applies to R-06 (incident INC-01 on the web shop in March, readiness LOW) and to R-02 (incident INC-04 in September, readiness LOW). It does not apply to R-08: its score is 12.

      The result is a ranked list that starts with three P1 risks due by November 21, 2026 — the CRITICAL R-01 and the two escalated HIGH risks — followed by four P2 risks due by December 14, 2026.

      Threat signals: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System), EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System), KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) and SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization)

      ▣ Slide 43 — Threat signals: CVSS, EPSS, KEV and SSVC

      When a risk depends on a software vulnerability, four public signals help to judge how urgent it is. They feed the likelihood justification and the “threat evidence” key; none of them replaces the register.

      • CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (FIRST) — a score from 0 to 10 for the technical severity of a vulnerability. FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) states that base scores measure severity and should not be used alone to assess risk: a 9.8 on a disconnected test camera can matter less than a 6.5 on the web shop.
      • EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (FIRST) — an estimated probability, from 0 to 1, that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days: a likelihood signal.
      • KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) (CISA catalogue) — the list of vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild. CVE-2017-7921, which affects Kalmia's cameras CAM-HQ-3 and CAM-HQ-4, was added on March 5, 2026.
      • SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) (CISA, developed with the SEI [Software Engineering Institute, Carnegie Mellon University]) — a decision tree that answers “what do we do?” with four outcomes — Track, Track*, Attend, Act — from exploitation status, technical impact, automatability, mission prevalence and public well-being impact.

      Notice the order of the questions: CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) asks how bad a weakness is, EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) how likely it is to be used soon, KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) whether it is already used, and SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) what to do about it. A risk-based priority needs all of them plus the business context of the register.

      Communicating the priorities: the top five

      ▣ Slide 44 — Communicating the priorities: the top five for Nadia Roy

      Prioritization ends with a short message to the people who decide. Nadia Roy receives the top-five list: for each risk, its rank and level, the consequence in plain language, the owner, the deadline and the first action being considered. Technical identifiers — CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) numbers, vectors, host names — go into an annex, not into the body of the message.

      Kalmia's top five are R-01, R-06, R-02, R-08, R-07. Together they cover the two scenarios that can stop the company (ransomware and the loss of NAS-01), the two personal-information risks that create Law 25 duties, and the production line. The message is confidential: it describes exactly where the company is weak (general criterion “respect for the confidentiality of analysis results”; Legal Notice, section 17).

      Key terms to learn

      ▣ Slide 45 — Key terms — Lesson 3
      Prioritization
      The documented ordering of risks for treatment, so that the greatest potential harm to the most important assets is treated first.
      Priority versus level
      The level comes from the matrix; the priority also uses asset criticality, threat evidence, readiness and deadlines.
      Lexicographic ordering
      Sorting on a first criterion and using the next one only to separate risks that are equal on all previous criteria.
      Tie-breaker
      A criterion used to order two risks with the same score: impact, criticality, evidence, readiness.
      Asset criticality
      How much the business depends on an asset (3 critical, 2 important, 1 limited), from the Lab 1 business impact analysis.
      Threat evidence
      Proof that a threat is active: KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) listing, observed attempts, a recent incident on the asset, or success in a test.
      Priority class
      P1 to P4, each with a deadline taken from the risk appetite.
      Escalation rule
      Kalmia course rule: a HIGH risk with score ≥ 15, active threat evidence and LOW readiness becomes P1.
      CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)
      A 0–10 score of the technical severity of a vulnerability; not a risk rating by itself.
      EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System)
      The estimated probability that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be exploited in the next 30 days.
      KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) catalog
      CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, United States)'s list of vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild.
      SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization)
      A decision tree with four outcomes (Track, Track*, Attend, Act) for vulnerability response.
      Top-five list
      The short, plain-language list of the highest-priority risks given to the decision-maker.

      Micro-activity — Break the tie (2 min)

      ▣ Slide 46 — Micro-activity — Break the tie (2 min)

      R-03 (fraudulent bank change: L3 × I3 = 9, criticality 2, evidence INC-02, readiness MODERATE) and R-11 (sales laptop lost: L3 × I3 = 9, criticality 1, no evidence, readiness LOW). Which one goes first, and which key decides?

      Show the answer

      R-03 goes first. Class (P3), score (9) and impact (3) are equal; the fourth key, asset criticality, decides: supplier payments (2) are more critical than the sales laptops (1). The later keys are not needed.

      Task of the example

      Rank the twelve register rows with Kalmia's documented method — class, score, impact, asset criticality, threat evidence, readiness — apply the escalation rule, assign the priority classes and their deadlines from the risk appetite, and produce the top-five list for Nadia Roy.

      How it relates to this lecture

      This is Lesson 3 applied: priority versus level, lexicographic ordering, tie-breakers, the escalation rule, threat signals (INC-, MR-, KEV [Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog]), and communication of the top five.

Lab 4: treatment actions are planned in this order. Class 15: “priority management: what to fix first and why”.

      The top five for Nadia Roy are R-01 (ransomware on NAS-01), R-06 (web shop account), R-02 (loyalty export), R-08 (NAS-01 disk failure) and R-07 (ROAST-PC remote access). Three of them are P1 with a deadline of November 21, 2026. Notice what the method changed compared with a simple sort by score: R-06 moved above R-02 because the web shop is a critical asset; R-08 moved above R-07 because its weakness is already showing errors; R-05 moved above R-04 because its consequence is severe even though it is rare. Every move can be explained in one sentence — the property a method must have.

      Interactive example 3 — Risk prioritizer with step-by-step sorting (self-contained HTML [HyperText Markup Language])

      ▣ Slide 49 — Interactive example 3 — the prioritizer (self-contained HTML)
      Task of the code

      The page computes the score, level and priority class of each risk, applies the escalation rule, then sorts the twelve risks with an insertion sort whose every comparison is shown: the two risks compared, the key that decides, and the move. It ends with the ranked list, the deadlines and the top five, and exports priority_list.csv. It can also load the CSV (comma-separated values) export of your own Lab 3 register.

      How it relates to the lecture

      It makes Lesson 3 visible: you watch the tie-breakers decide, one comparison at a time, and you can switch the escalation rule off to see its effect.

      Interactive example 3 — Risk prioritizer with step-by-step sorting (self-contained HTML [HyperText Markup Language])
      The code of the example — a comment before every line (click to show or hide; use Copy code above)
      Step by step — what the code does
      1. The page holds the twelve risks as data: identifier, short name, likelihood, impact, asset criticality, threat evidence, readiness and owner.
      2. Plan: for each risk it computes the score (likelihood × impact), the level (bands of Lesson 2) and the base class (CRITICAL → P1 … LOW → P4), and logs one step per risk.
      3. It applies the escalation rule to every HIGH risk: score of 15 or more, threat evidence and LOW readiness give P1; each check is logged with its result.
      4. It sorts with an insertion sort: each new risk is compared with the risk above it; compare() walks the keys in order (class, score, impact, criticality, evidence, readiness, identifier) and returns the first key that differs — that key is written in the log.
      5. Each comparison is a step: the bars of the two risks are highlighted and, if the order changes, the bars swap places on the chart.
      6. When the sort ends, the page numbers the ranks, computes each deadline from November 14, 2026 (7, 30, 90 or 365 days), fills the result table and highlights the top five.
      7. Start runs the steps on a timer; Pause stops after the current step so that the log can be read; Step advances by one; Restart rebuilds the plan from the beginning. The speed slider changes the delay.
      8. The checkbox switches the escalation rule on or off; the plan is rebuilt so that the class can see which risks move.
      9. “Load my CSV (comma-separated values)” reads a register exported from the Lab 3 workbook (columns risk_id, short, likelihood, impact, criticality, threat_evidence, readiness, owner) and ranks it with the same method — title lines, empty template rows and semicolon-separated files are handled; “Download CSV” saves the ranked list.

      Recap — five sentences to keep
      ▣ Slide 53 — Recap — five sentences to keep
      1. Response capability mainly changes impact: outage ≈ detect + contain + recover, compared with the MTD (maximum tolerable downtime).
      2. Readiness is scored on evidence (0 absent → 3 tested); Kalmia today: 5/24, LOW.
      3. The matrix shows the picture; the register keeps the reasons — L, I, justification, evidence, owner.
      4. A priority is not a level: class, score, impact, criticality, evidence, readiness — in that order.
      5. No owner, no rank, no decision: evidence · owner · rank.

      Key terms
      Asset criticality (L3) — How much the business depends on an asset (3 critical, 2 important, 1 limited), from the Lab 1 business impact analysis.
      Band (L2) — A range of scores that receives one level and one decision rule (LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL).
      Confidentiality incident (L1) — Under Québec law: unauthorized access to, use or communication of personal information, or its loss.
      CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) (L3) — A 0–10 score of the technical severity of a vulnerability; not a risk rating by itself.
      Cybersecurity risk register (CSRR [cybersecurity risk register]) (L2) — NIST (National Institute of Standards and Technology, United States)'s name for the register of cybersecurity risks that rolls up into the enterprise register.
      EPSS (Exploit Prediction Scoring System) (L3) — The estimated probability that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be exploited in the next 30 days.
      Escalation rule (L3) — Kalmia course rule: a HIGH risk with score ≥ 15, active threat evidence and LOW readiness becomes P1.
      Incident response (L1) — The organized actions taken to detect, analyze, contain, eradicate, recover from and learn from an incident.
      Incident response plan (IRP [incident response plan]) (L1) — The written and approved document that sets roles, contacts, decisions, steps and communications for incidents.
      Inherent / current / residual / target risk (L2) — Risk without controls / with today's controls / after treatment / desired level by a date.
      KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) catalog (L3) — CISA (Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, United States)'s list of vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild.
      Lexicographic ordering (L3) — Sorting on a first criterion and using the next one only to separate risks that are equal on all previous criteria.
      MTD (maximum tolerable downtime) (L1) — The longest time a business process can be unavailable before the harm becomes unacceptable; the RTO (recovery time objective) must be shorter.
      MTTD (mean time to detect) / MTTC (mean time to contain) / MTTR (mean time to recover) (L1) — Average times to detect, to contain and to recover; their sum approximates the outage.
      Ordinal scale (L2) — A scale whose numbers give an order but not a distance; multiplying ordinal levels is a convention.
      Playbook (L1) — A step-by-step procedure for one type of incident, for example ransomware.
      Prioritization (L3) — The documented ordering of risks for treatment, so that the greatest potential harm to the most important assets is treated first.
      Priority class (L3) — P1 to P4, each with a deadline taken from the risk appetite.
      Priority versus level (L3) — The level comes from the matrix; the priority also uses asset criticality, threat evidence, readiness and deadlines.
      Range compression (L2) — Different risks receiving the same cell or band, which hides real differences between them.
      Readiness score (L1) — Course rule: sum of eight maturity scores (0–3) divided by 24; LOW, MODERATE or HIGH.
      Register of confidentiality incidents (L1) — The legal register every Québec enterprise keeps of all its confidentiality incidents.
      Response capability (L1) — The people, processes, technology and partners that let an organization respond; a set of detective and corrective controls that mainly reduces impact.
      Review date (L2) — The date on which a row must be re-assessed; part of the follow-up columns.
      Risk appetite (L2) — The amount and type of risk an organization is willing to pursue or retain.
      Risk matrix (heat map) (L2) — A grid crossing likelihood and impact levels; each cell receives a risk level.
      Risk owner (L2) — The manager accountable for a risk and authorized to decide about it.
      Risk register (L2) — A record of information about identified risks; the one table where risks are described, rated, owned and followed.
      Risk scenario statement (L2) — One sentence naming threat source, event, risk factor, asset and consequence.
      Risk tolerance (L2) — The readiness to bear a risk after treatment; a narrower limit for one objective or category.
      RTO (recovery time objective) / RPO (recovery point objective) (L1) — Target time to restore a process; maximum acceptable data loss measured in time.
      Security event (L1) — Any observable occurrence in a system or a network; most events are harmless.
      Security incident (L1) — An occurrence that actually or imminently jeopardizes the confidentiality, integrity or availability of information or a system, or violates a security policy.
      SSVC (Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization) (L3) — A decision tree with four outcomes (Track, Track*, Attend, Act) for vulnerability response.
      Tabletop exercise (TTX [tabletop exercise]) (L1) — A discussion-based exercise in which the team walks through a scenario to test the plan.
      Threat evidence (L3) — Proof that a threat is active: KEV (Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog) listing, observed attempts, a recent incident on the asset, or success in a test.
      Tie-breaker (L3) — A criterion used to order two risks with the same score: impact, criticality, evidence, readiness.
      Top-five list (L3) — The short, plain-language list of the highest-priority risks given to the decision-maker.

      • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Developing your incident response plan (ITSAP.40.003, updated January 2026) — What a plan contains: team and backup contacts, policy, communications, response steps, backups, training and exercises. VirusTotal check
      • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Report a cyber incident — The online form organizations in Canada use to report a cyber incident. VirusTotal check
      • Canadian Centre for Cyber Security — Baseline cyber security controls for small and medium organizations — Control BC.1 (develop an incident response plan) and control BC.7 (back up and encrypt data; verify recovery). VirusTotal check
      • CIS Critical Security Control 17 — Incident Response Management — The CIS (Center for Internet Security) Control that describes an incident response capability: policies, plans, roles, training, communication. VirusTotal check
      Privacy law
      • LégisQuébec — Act respecting the protection of personal information in the private sector (CQLR, c. P-39.1) — Sections 3.5 to 3.8: confidentiality incidents, notification of the CAI (Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec, the Québec privacy regulator) and of the persons concerned, the register of incidents. VirusTotal check
      • Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec (CAI) — The Québec privacy regulator, which receives notices of confidentiality incidents that present a risk of serious injury. VirusTotal check
      • Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada — What you need to know about mandatory reporting of breaches of security safeguards — PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act): report breaches that create a real risk of significant harm, notify individuals, keep records of every breach for two years. VirusTotal check
      Risk matrix and register
      • NIST SP 800-30 Revision 1 — Guide for Conducting Risk Assessments (2012) — Example likelihood, impact and risk scales and the level-of-risk table (Appendices G, H and I). VirusTotal check
      • NIST IR 8286 Revision 1 — Integrating Cybersecurity and Enterprise Risk Management (December 2025) — How cybersecurity risk registers feed the enterprise risk register; supersedes the 2020 edition. VirusTotal check
      • NIST IR 8286A Revision 1 — Identifying and Estimating Cybersecurity Risk for ERM (December 2025) — Documenting risk scenarios and recording their likelihood and impact in cybersecurity risk registers; publishes a risk register schema. VirusTotal check
      • ISO 31000:2018 — Risk management — Guidelines — The general risk-management process; defines a control as a measure that maintains or modifies risk. VirusTotal check
      • ISO 31073:2022 — Risk management — Vocabulary — The vocabulary of risk management: risk register, risk owner, risk appetite, risk tolerance, residual risk. VirusTotal check
      • ISO/IEC 27005:2022 — Guidance on managing information security risks — Information-security risk assessment and treatment; leaves the choice of scales and criteria to the organization. VirusTotal check
      • OWASP Risk Rating Methodology — A 0-to-9 likelihood and impact method with a 3 × 3 severity table and a step called 'deciding what to fix'. VirusTotal check
      • Cox, L. A. (2008) — What's Wrong with Risk Matrices? Risk Analysis 28(2), 497–512 — Peer-reviewed article on the mathematical limits of risk matrices: poor resolution, range compression and possible ranking errors. VirusTotal check
      Prioritization
      • NIST IR 8286B Update 1 — Prioritizing Cybersecurity Risk for Enterprise Risk Management (February 2025) — The priority of each risk is set in light of its potential impact on enterprise objectives and recorded in the register. VirusTotal check
      • CISA — Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog — Vulnerabilities with evidence of exploitation in the wild; CVE-2017-7921 (Kalmia's cameras) was added on March 5, 2026. VirusTotal check
      • FIRST — Exploit Prediction Scoring System (EPSS) — Estimates the probability that a published CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) will be exploited in the wild in the next 30 days. VirusTotal check
      • FIRST — Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) — Severity scores of vulnerabilities; FIRST (Forum of Incident Response and Security Teams) states that base scores measure severity and should not be used alone to assess risk. VirusTotal check
      • CISA — Stakeholder-Specific Vulnerability Categorization (SSVC) — A decision tree (Track, Track*, Attend, Act) built on exploitation status, technical impact, automatability, mission prevalence and public well-being impact. VirusTotal check

      • Incident Planning — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 4.8 (Professor Messer, 6:50) — How tabletop exercises, walkthroughs and simulations test a response plan before a real incident: the evidence behind a score of 3 on the readiness scale. VirusTotal check
      • Business Impact Analysis — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 5.2 (Professor Messer, 2:55) — RTO (recovery time objective), RPO (recovery point objective), MTTR (mean time to recover) and MTBF in three minutes: the time measures that tell whether a response is fast enough. VirusTotal check
      • Risk Analysis — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 5.2 (Professor Messer, 9:13) — Qualitative and quantitative assessment, risk appetite versus risk tolerance, and the risk register with its owners and indicators. VirusTotal check
      • Risk Management — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 5.2 (Professor Messer, 3:30) — Risk identification and the different types of risk assessment (one-time, recurring, continuous): why a register is reviewed on a schedule. VirusTotal check
      • Analyzing Vulnerabilities — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 4.3 (Professor Messer, 10:29) — Why a CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score is not a priority: false positives, exposure, environmental variables and risk tolerance decide what is fixed first. VirusTotal check
      • Risk Management Strategies — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 5.2 (Professor Messer, 3:12) — Transfer, accept, avoid and mitigate: what happens to a risk after it has been prioritized (the bridge to Topic 6 on Monday). VirusTotal check
      • Vulnerability Remediation — CompTIA Security+ SY0-701 — 4.3 (Professor Messer, 8:45) — Patching, insurance, segmentation and compensating controls, and how exceptions are documented when a fix must wait. VirusTotal check
